p: Turning up prepared makes all the difference between a brilliant session and a soggy, chilly one. Here's what's worth bringing: gloves (non-negotiable), a warm but not bulky layer, long socks that come up past the top of the boot and trousers that won't mind a bit of damp. A small bag or zipped pockets keep phones and keys safe, because anything that slips out on the ice tends to go sliding.

Once you're in your hire skates, take a minute to check the fit. Tight around the ankle, snug at the heel, toes able to wriggle a little. Loose boots make it much harder to balance, so ask for a different size if they don't feel right. The staff are used to it.

Beginners, start by marching on the spot at the barrier, then try small gliding steps. Bend your knees, keep your chin up and resist the urge to stare at your feet. You'll be amazed how quickly it starts to click.

The south side of Leeds has a few handy extras nearby. The White Rose shopping centre is close to the rink for food and a browse, and Middleton Park, one of the city's big green spaces, has woodland walks and the Middleton Railway, one of the oldest railways in the world, on its doorstep. Further out, Temple Newsam is a grand Tudor-Jacobean house with a huge estate and a working farm, making a great family follow-up to a morning on the ice.
